description: How Bovell weaves naturalistic dialogue with direct-address monologues, and how movement carries subtext.
content_html:
Two Languages in One Play

Andrew Bovell gives Things I Know to Be True two distinct theatrical languages that work in counterpoint throughout the play. The first is naturalistic family dialogue — the everyday speech of a suburban household, full of interruptions, silences and unfinished thoughts. The second is a more openly theatrical language: direct address monologue and stylised physical movement. Understanding how Bovell moves between these two registers — and what that movement achieves for the audience — is central to answering any question about dramatic methods in this play.

The alternation is structural. Naturalistic scenes establish the domestic reality of the Price family: their relationships, their habits, the particular tensions of a household where four adult children are still emotionally tied to parents who are themselves imperfect. Then, at moments of heightened emotion, the register shifts. A character steps outside the scene to speak directly to the audience, or the family moves into a Frantic Assembly movement sequence that says in bodies what cannot be said in words.

Key Fact

Bovell uses two theatrical registers: naturalistic dialogue (characters speak to each other as real people might) and direct address (a character speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the scene). Moving between these registers is itself a dramatic method.

Rosie and the Art of Direct Address

Rosie functions as the play’s primary narrator-figure. Her monologue passages are spoken from a temporal position that is partly outside the action: she often knows, or half-knows, what the season will bring. This creates a layer of dramatic irony — the audience senses things will go wrong before they do, sharing a partial foreknowledge with Rosie that the other characters do not have.

In production, the staging of Rosie’s direct-address passages must communicate her dual temporal position. A director might place her at upstage centre while the family activity continues downstage, visually separating her narrator-self from her character-self. A lighting designer might use a tight lighting special to pull her out of the general lighting wash, signalling to the audience that she is speaking from a different register of truth.

Students sometimes treat Rosie’s direct-address passages as straightforward narration — a way of telling the audience what is happening. This misreads their function. Rosie’s monologues carry subtext: they express what she feels but cannot say to the family, and they position the audience as her confidant rather than a detached observer. As a performer playing Rosie, you are not reporting; you are sharing something that costs you emotionally. The vocal and physical choices must reflect that emotional cost. Speaking at a steady, measured pace with a slightly lower volume than the dialogue scenes suggests intimacy; allowing brief pauses before key revelations gives the audience space to feel the weight of what is coming.

Movement as Subtext: The Frantic Assembly Sequences

The physical theatre sequences in Things I Know to Be True were developed in collaboration with Frantic Assembly, the British physical theatre company co-directed by Scott Graham. Frantic Assembly’s approach to movement is rooted in everyday physicality rather than stylised dance: they build sequences from contact improvisation, counter-balance, and the reordering of familiar gestures. The result is movement that feels emotionally urgent rather than aesthetically decorative.

In this play, the movement sequences function as heightened subtext. When the Price family’s emotional life exceeds what their naturalistic dialogue can hold, Bovell’s stage directions call for a physical sequence. These moments might involve a lift that expresses both love and the effort of holding a relationship together, a chair duet that externalises a conversation neither character can have in words, or the round-by-through-under contact work in which bodies pass through each other’s space, suggesting emotional entanglement.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly movement sequences in the play externalise subtext: the things characters feel but cannot verbalise. A lift might express the effort of parental love; a chair duet might show the negotiation inside a relationship. The movement is not illustrative — it reveals.

The Garden Monologue and Rose Imagery

Bob’s rose garden is not simply a set piece; it is a recurring motif that carries a great deal of the play’s emotional weight without being stated directly. When Bob speaks in or near the garden — tending, pruning, simply being — the garden becomes the physical correlative of his inner life: ordered, carefully maintained, beautiful in a way that the rest of his world is not. In staging terms, a sound designer might build a subtle soundscape for the garden: birdsong, a light breeze, the distant sound of cicadas in summer — sounds that contrast with the harder, closer acoustic of the kitchen interior.

The rose imagery also works in conjunction with mood and atmosphere. In spring, the roses are beginning: fresh colour, the optimism of new growth. By winter, bare stems. A designer who makes the rose bush a visible element of the set can track this seasonal arc visually, so that the garden itself becomes a kind of scenic narrator — telling the audience where in the emotional year they are without any dialogue needing to do that work.

As a performer delivering a direct-address monologue, you face a specific challenge: you are speaking to the audience, not to another character, so the usual triggers of reaction and response are removed. To hold this, you must anchor each moment in a specific thought or feeling. Vocally, you might use a slower pace than the dialogue scenes, a slightly raised head so that eye-line reaches out across the auditorium, and variation in volume — dropping to near-quiet for the most privately held thoughts. Physically, stillness is a powerful choice: if the rest of the production is in motion, a still figure speaking directly out commands attention.

As a lighting designer, a direct-address monologue offers the chance to make a distinct visual statement. Removing the character from the general wash and placing them in a tight profile spot — a warm amber or a cooler neutral depending on the season — signals the change in register without any spoken announcement. If the family remains dimly visible upstage in a reduced wash while Rosie speaks downstage in a special, the audience holds two simultaneous spaces: the world of the family and the world of the narrator. This dual focus is one of the most effective staging solutions for the monologue moments.
exam_tip_html:
For the 12-mark question on playwright’s intentions, a common error is to treat direct address and movement sequences as separate topics rather than analysing them as two parts of the same dramatic method: both are ways Bovell controls the audience’s relationship to the action. Ask yourself: what does Bovell want the audience to feel at the moment Rosie steps outside the scene? What does he want them to feel during a movement sequence? Your answer must address the intended effect on the audience, not just describe the technique.

For the 20-mark extended staging response, do not separate performer and designer as though they belong to different questions. The strongest answers show how a performer’s stillness during direct address is amplified by a lighting special, or how a movement sequence gains meaning because the soundscape shifts to something non-diegetic and abstract. Every staging choice in a movement sequence should be justified with reference to the specific emotional moment it represents.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bovell writes in two theatrical registers: naturalistic dialogue and direct-address monologue / stylised movement. The shift between them is itself a dramatic method, signalling to the audience that the play is moving into a different kind of truth.
  • Rosie’s direct-address monologues create dramatic irony: she speaks from partial foreknowledge, making the audience share a sense of what is coming before it arrives. As a performer, this demands holding two timeframes in the body simultaneously.
  • Frantic Assembly movement sequences externalise subtext — the emotional content that dialogue cannot contain. The rose garden’s soundscape and lighting state can reinforce the seasonal arc, giving the play a visual and auditory narrative that runs in parallel to the spoken one.

practice_questions.text: Name the physical theatre company whose techniques Bovell incorporated into Things I Know to Be True.
What is meant by the term 'subtext' in drama?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. the meaning beneath the surface of the dialogue, what is implied rather than stated); 1 mark for development showing understanding of how subtext functions in performance (e.g. what characters feel but cannot say, communicated through pause, physicality or the gap between words and action).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses Rosie's direct-address monologues to position the audience differently from the other characters on stage.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of Rosie as the narrator-figure who speaks directly to the audience (1); explanation of the temporal complexity of her monologues (partial foreknowledge, dual time frame) (1); explanation of how this creates dramatic irony for the audience (1); reference to the effect this has on the audience's emotional experience of the revelations as they arrive (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of using a Frantic Assembly movement sequence in place of naturalistic dialogue at a moment of high emotional intensity. How might a lighting designer enhance this effect?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that movement sequences externalise subtext or feelings that words cannot contain; 1 mark for a specific lighting choice (e.g. removing the general wash and using a single moving light to follow the performers, or allowing a soundscape to carry the scene while lighting dims to near-blackout); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on the audience at that moment; 1 mark for linking the choice to the emotional content of the specific scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses direct-address monologue and physical movement as dramatic methods to communicate meaning that naturalistic dialogue alone cannot achieve. Consider what each method allows the playwright to do and what effect it creates for the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of Bovell's intentions in using both direct address and physical movement, explaining that each serves a different but complementary purpose. Direct address: positions the audience as confidant, creates dramatic irony, allows temporal complexity. Movement: externalises subtext, communicates what words cannot. Both are read as deliberate alternatives to naturalism, not incidental features. The student makes clear what the playwright wants the audience to feel at these heightened moments. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies both direct address and movement sequences, explains the function of each with some reference to audience effect. May not fully explore the temporal complexity of the monologues but shows clear understanding that these methods serve the play's emotional architecture.

Developing: Describes what direct address and movement sequences look like rather than analysing what Bovell intends them to achieve. Some audience effect mentioned but largely descriptive.

Emerging: Names one or both techniques with little or no analysis of playwright intention or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging a Frantic Assembly movement sequence during a moment when two members of the Price family are unable to speak to each other directly, explain how you would use the movement itself, the soundscape, and a lighting choice to communicate the emotional content of the moment to the audience. Refer to specific staging decisions and their intended effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific movement vocabulary described (e.g. a contact-improvised lift that expresses the effort of holding a relationship together, or a chair duet in which one performer pursues and the other retreats); soundscape: named texture (e.g. a low, non-diegetic underscore that builds in volume and then cuts to silence at the peak of the sequence); lighting: specific choice (e.g. a slow cross-fade from a warm amber wash to a cooler blue as the sequence intensifies, using a gobo to project fractured light across the stage). Every choice anchored to the emotional content with a clear explanation of intended audience effect.

Secure: Most disciplines addressed; at least one named lighting choice and one specific description of the movement; soundscape present but possibly generic; audience effect mostly addressed.

Developing: Relevant ideas but described in general terms (e.g. 'dramatic music', 'slow movement'); limited reference to named staging elements; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging: List of ideas without justification; no reference to specific staging choices; mostly descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the primary function of Rosie's direct-address monologues in Things I Know to Be True?
options: To summarise the plot for the audience
To position the audience as her confidant and create dramatic irony
To give information about other characters' backstories
To replace naturalistic dialogue in the kitchen scenes

knowledge_checks.q: Which physical theatre company co-developed Things I Know to Be True with Andrew Bovell?
The implied or unstated meaning beneath the surface dialogue of a scene is called _____.
A broad, even distribution of light covering the whole stage is called a lighting _____.
Match each dramatic method to its function in Things I Know to Be True:
right: Positions the audience as confidant; creates dramatic irony
Externalises subtext too intense for spoken language
Establishes the domestic reality of the Price family

flashcard_questions.q: What is direct address in drama?
flashcard_questions.a: A character speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the action of the scene.
A speech delivered by one performer alone, either to the audience or as private reflection.
The implied meaning beneath the surface dialogue — what characters feel but do not say.
When the audience knows something one or more characters on stage do not yet know.
A focused light directed at one performer, isolating them from the general stage wash.
A broad, even distribution of light across the whole stage or a large area of it.
A continuous layer of ambient sound built from multiple elements to create atmosphere.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a chair duet in Frantic Assembly's vocabulary?
flashcard_questions.a: Two performers using chairs as contact-improvisation props, creating lifts and counter-balance.

flashcard_questions.q: Which character in Things I Know to Be True delivers direct-address monologues as a narrator-figure?
Why does Bovell use Frantic Assembly movement sequences rather than dialogue at emotional peaks?
flashcard_questions.a: To externalise subtext — feelings too intense to be expressed in words alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What symbolic object is associated with Bob's emotional life throughout the play?
What is mood and atmosphere in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The emotional climate created for the audience through all theatrical elements working together.

glossary_terms.definition: A speech in which a character addresses the audience directly, stepping outside the action of the scene and breaking the illusion of a fourth wall.
A speech delivered by one performer alone, either to the audience or as a form of private reflection made public.
A dramatic device in which the audience possesses information that one or more characters on stage do not yet have.
The area of the stage furthest from the audience, away from the front edge.
The area of the stage closest to the audience, at the front edge.
A focused beam of light directed at a specific performer or area of the stage, isolating them from their surroundings.
A broad, even distribution of light across the whole stage or a large section of it.
The implied or unstated meaning beneath the surface dialogue or action of a scene; what characters feel but do not say.
A Frantic Assembly technique in which two performers work with chairs as contact-improvisation props, creating lifts, slides and counter-balance sequences.
A continuous layer of ambient sound constructed from multiple recorded or live elements to create atmosphere or environment.
Mood and atmosphere created through all the theatrical elements working together to produce a specific emotional climate in the audience.
